About: a point-mass gravitational lens and the images it makes of a star behind it

About this simulation

On screen
Main view: a side view with the observer O, the lens L at DL = 4 kpc and the source S at DS = 8 kpc. Two rays from S bend at the lens plane, one above L and one below, and dashed sight lines from O end at the images (open circles) on the source plane. To the right, the sky seen from O on the same vertical scale, −4 to +4 mas: the lens, the dashed Einstein ring, the true source (blue cross) and the images. Below: the image positions θ against β, with the dashed line θ = β.
Controls
β sets the angle of the source from the line OL, −2.50 to +2.50 mas. M sets the lens mass, 0.25 to 4 M☉; changing it greys the traces so far. Slide carries the source at 0.5 mas per second towards +2.50 mas, holding 1 s at β = 0; press it again, or touch a slider, to stop; from +2.50 mas it starts again at −2.50 mas.
Readouts
In the sidebar: β and θE; the image angles θ+ and θ−, the roots of θ2 − βθ − θE2 = 0, and their separation (from card 4); the magnification of each image, μ = |1 − (θE/θ)4|−1, and of both together; and the ring radius at the lens, DLθE in AU, beside Jupiter's orbit for scale.
Model
A point-mass lens and a point source, in the thin-lens and small-angle approximations, with the bending 4GM/(c2b) at b = DL|θ| and θE2 = (4GM/c2)DLS/(DLDS). The distances are fixed, so θE ∝ √M here; at other distances the same mass gives a different ring. A real source has a finite size, so its ring has a width and its magnification stays finite at β = 0.
A Star Behind a Star
Side view and the sky seen from Oheight = angle × distance; sky in mas
Image positionsθ+ and θ− against β
Not to scale
The heights are stretched enormously compared with the distances along the axis, and the sky panel is magnified enormously: the images lie about two thousandths of a second of arc apart, too close for ordinary telescopes to separate. Surveys see their combined brightening instead (the magnification readouts); only optical interferometers have resolved a few such pairs.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A source beside the lens

Keep the lens mass at 1 M☉ and set β to +1.00 mas. Before looking at the sky panel, predict what the observer sees.

2 · A source right behind the lens

Keep the lens mass at 1 M☉ and set β to 0, so that the source is exactly behind the lens. Before looking at the sky panel, predict what the observer sees.

3 · Sliding the source across

Keep the lens mass at 1 M☉ and set β to −2.50 mas. You will press Slide, which carries the source across behind the lens to +2.50 mas. Before you do, predict what happens to the two images as the source passes behind the lens.

4 · Separation of the images

Keep the lens mass at 1 M☉ and set β to 0. You will move β slowly up to +2.50 mas, watching the separation readout and the image-position graph. Before you do, predict how the separation of the two images changes.

5 · Where the images lie

Keep the lens mass at 1 M☉ and β at +2.50 mas, which is about two and a half Einstein radii. Before comparing the readouts, predict where the two images lie.

6 · A heavier lens

Set β to 0 and the lens mass to 1 M☉, so that the ring has radius 1.01 mas. You will raise the mass to 4 M☉. Before you do, predict the new radius of the ring.

7 · What a point lens does

A point mass bends a passing ray by 4GM/(c2b), so a source behind it is seen twice: one image outside the Einstein ring on the source's side and one inside it on the other, at the roots of θ2 − βθ − θE2 = 0.

Perfect alignment turns the two images into a ring of radius θE, with θE2 = (4GM/c2)DLS/(DLDS): at fixed distances the ring grows as √M.

For a star lensing a star the images are only about 2 mas apart, so surveys usually see their combined light instead: the total magnification rises to a peak as the source passes behind the lens, a microlensing event.

A Star Behind a Star

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A star far behind another star is almost, but not exactly, in line with us. This sim shows the arrangement from the side and as the sky looks from the observer, and lets you slide the distant star sideways and change the mass of the star in front.

What you'll learn

  • How a mass bends a passing ray, and the equation that links angles on the sky.
  • What the observer sees as the source moves behind the lens.
  • How bright it looks, and what sets the size of the pattern.
  • What this tells us about unseen mass.
The sim's views, as it opens: side view with the three distances, and the sky panel with the lens, the dashed circle and the source.

What's on screen

  • Side view: observer O, lens L at DL = 4 kpc and source S at DS = 8 kpc. Angles are in milliarcseconds (mas, 10−3 arcsec).
  • Sky panel, ±4 mas across: the lens at the centre, a dashed circle of radius θE, and a blue cross where the source truly lies.
  • Graph of image angle against source angle, with the dashed line θ = β for no lens. Readouts group the angles, the brightness and the ring size.
See itLook at the opening view. Watch for: the source sitting well to one side of the dashed circle, and the readouts at β = −2.50 mas.

03

Bending and the lens equation tie the angles together

A ray passing a mass M at impact parameter b is bent towards it through the angle (notes, eq. 9.26), valid when b is much larger than 2GM/c²:

Equation (9.26). 4GM/c² is the length scale of the lens.

For M = 1 M☉, 4GM/c² is 5.9 km, so a ray passing at b = 4.04 AU is bent by 2.02 mas.

The ray that reaches O at angle θ passes the lens plane at b = DLθ. At the distance of the source, the heights θDS of the image and βDS of the source differ by the shift α̂DLS that the bending produces. Putting θDS = βDS + α̂DLS and α̂ = 4GM/(c²DLθ) gives the lens equation (eq. 9.27):

Equation (9.27), the lens equation, and the Einstein radius θE. Angles are small, so tan θ ≈ θ.
One ray, with heights exaggerated. The ray reaching O at angle θ passes the lens plane at b = DLθ, where it is bent through α̂. The source lies at angle β.

θE is set by the mass and the three distances. In the sim, θE = 1.01 mas at M = 1 M☉, which is 4.04 AU at the lens.

Key idea. Bending falls as 1/b, so the lens equation has a term −θE²/θ that shrinks as θ grows.
04

Two images from one source, one on each side of the lens

Multiplying the lens equation by θ gives θ² − βθ − θE² = 0, whose roots are (eq. 9.28):

Equation (9.28). The square root is larger than |β|, so the signs of θ+ and θ− are fixed.

The roots multiply to −θE², so they have opposite signs: there is one image on each side of the lens. For β > 0, θ+ lies outside the ring on the source's side, and θ− inside it on the other side. For β < 0 the roles swap. Neither image crosses the lens: θ+ stays positive and θ− stays negative.

At β = +1.00 mas and M = 1 M☉, θ+ = +1.63 mas and θ− = −0.63 mas, passing the lens at 6.51 AU and 2.50 AU. At β = 2.50 mas they are +2.86 and −0.36 mas, close to β + θE²/β and −θE²/β: the outer image just beyond the source, the inner one near the lens.

05

Ring and sliding: a ring behind the lens, and the two images swap sides

With β = 0 the arrangement is the same all round the line O–L, so the image is a ring of radius θE: the roots are ±θE, and rays pass the lens at DLθE = 4.04 AU on every side. The sim shows μ as ∞ (ring) there.

Away from the axis, θ+ − θ− = √(β² + 4θE²). The separation is smallest, 2θE = 2.02 mas, at β = 0 and grows steadily to 3.21 mas at β = 2.50 mas.

Sliding from β = −2.50 mas, the two images close in on the ring, the outer one moving in and the inner one moving out. At β = 0 they spread into the ring. After that, the image that was inside moves out through the ring and the one that was outside moves in.

Image angle θ against source angle β at M = 1 M☉. The two branches never reach θ = 0.
See itSet β = 0 with M = 1 M☉. Watch for: μ reading ∞ (ring), the separation at 2.02 mas, and a solid cyan ring drawn on the dashed circle.
See itPress Slide from β = −2.50 mas. Watch for: the two circles closing on the dashed ring, merging into it at β = 0 after 5 s, then separating, with the dots on the graph tracing the two branches.
Key idea. Each branch crosses the ring radius once, at β = 0, and never reaches the lens itself.
06

How bright each image is, in proportion to its area on the sky

Intensity is constant along a ray (notes, §3.3), so each image has the surface brightness of the source, and its brightness follows its solid angle. The magnification of both images together is (eq. 9.34):

Equation (9.34). η is the source angle in units of the Einstein radius.

Each image has A± = y±²/(η√(η²+4)), with y± = θ±/θE (eq. 9.33). The sim's per-image readout, 1/|1 − (θE/θ)⁴|, is the same quantity written in terms of θ.

At β = 1.00 mas, η = 0.99: μ+ = 1.17, μ− = 0.17 and the total is 1.35. At β = 0.30 mas the total is 3.47 (2.24 and 1.24). As β → 0, the formula diverges for a point source. The outer image is always magnified, and the inner one may be fainter than the source.

Magnification against η, for the two images and for both together (curves from the sim's own formulas).
See itSet β = +0.30 mas with M = 1 M☉. Watch for: Both together μ jumping to 3.47×, with the two images close to the ring.
07

Mass and the size of the ring, which grows as the square root of M

Because θE² is proportional to M, quadrupling the mass doubles the ring: θE goes from 1.01 to 2.02 mas, and DLθE from 4.04 to 8.07 AU. The sim sets this against Jupiter's orbit, 5.2 AU.

The reason is that the ray reaching O at the ring must satisfy θDS = α̂DLS, so the bend must grow in proportion to b. The bend 4GM/(c²b) falls as b grows, so a heavier lens balances it at a larger b, with b² proportional to M.

An Einstein ring of measured radius gives the mass inside the cylinder of radius DLθE (eq. 9.29):

Equation (9.29), with θE in radians. It needs no assumption about how the matter moves.
See itSet β = 0 and raise M from 1 to 4 M☉. Watch for: θE rising to 2.02 mas, and the ring size to 8.07 AU, past the Jupiter value.
08

Where it matters

  • Mass without equilibrium. Behind rich clusters, background galaxies are stretched into arcs along the cluster's Einstein ring, with angular radii of tens of seconds of arc. Eq. 9.29 gives the mass inside the arcs, and it agrees with the virial and X-ray masses to within a factor of order one.
  • Looking for dark objects. In 1986 Paczyński pointed out that a body passing close to the line of sight to a star would brighten it for a while. For a lens in the halo and a star in the Large Magellanic Cloud, θE is less than a millisecond of arc, too small for the images to be told apart, and what is observed is their total brightness.
  • A brightening in time. As lens and star drift past each other, η falls and then rises, so the total A of eq. 9.34 rises and falls again (notes, Fig. 103).
Go deeper: what the sim leaves out
  • The sim uses ordinary distances and a point lens. For distant sources the notes say the distances must be defined with the metric of an expanding universe.
  • A lens with its mass spread over a region, not a point, deflects by 4GM(<b)/(c²b), where M(<b) is the mass inside the cylinder of radius b.
09

Summary

In one line. A mass bends a passing ray by 4GM/(c²b), and the lens equation β = θ − θE²/θ ties the angle at which a source is seen to its true angle, with θE set by the mass and the distances.

Key points

  • The roots of the lens equation are one image on each side of the lens.
  • Directly behind the lens the image is a ring of radius θE, proportional to √M.
  • Magnification is the ratio of areas on the sky, A = (η² + 2)/(η√(η² + 4)).

Common mix-ups

  • "A lens exactly in front of the source hides it." It makes a ring of the source's own light round the lens.
  • "Four times the mass gives four times the ring." The ring grows as √M, so ×2.
  • "The images pass through the lens as the source slides." θ+ stays above the lens and θ− below it throughout.

Things to try on your own

  • Set M = 2.25 and β = 0. Predict the ring radius, then check it (1.51 mas).
  • At β = 1.00 mas, check that θ+ × θ− = −θE².
